issues.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument whose recitals relinquish rights in immovable property cannot be used to prove the primary purpose of partition, even if it is described as a memorandum recording an earlier transaction.
material_facts: In a partition suit, the defendants sought to rely on two unregistered and unstamped documents as evidence that the properties had already been partitioned.
Although one document was described as recording an earlier partition, the recitals in both documents provided for relinquishment of rights in immovable property.
issues.conclusion: The documents were compulsorily registrable and inadmissible for proving the factum of partition as their primary purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908, a non-testamentary instrument that creates, declares, assigns, limits or extinguishes rights in immovable property must be registered; Section 49 bars an unregistered document from being received as evidence of a transaction affecting that property. The document’s title is not decisive: its nature and substance are determined from its terms, and admissibility depends on its recitals rather than the pleadings of the party tendering it.

predicates.partition_suit_evidence_issue: The instrument is tendered as evidence in a proceeding seeking partition of property.
predicates.instrument_relinquishes_immovable_proper: The instrument's recitals provide for relinquishment of rights in immovable property.
predicates.instrument_is_unregistered: The instrument has not been registered.

issues.definition: When an unregistered instrument that relinquishes rights in immovable property is tendered in a partition proceeding, it cannot prove the partition as its primary purpose.

issues.legal_issue: An unstamped and unregistered instrument may be received in a partition suit for a collateral purpose, but not to prove division of joint property by metes and bounds, and only subject to impounding, payment of stamp duty and penalty, proof, and relevance.
material_facts: The defendants alternatively sought to use the unregistered and unstamped documents for a collateral purpose.
The documents concerned an alleged earlier partition and the resulting shares and possession.
The court held that the documents could be marked for a collateral purpose after payment of stamp duty and penalty and impounding, subject to proof and relevance.
issues.conclusion: The documents were admissible for a collateral purpose subject to payment of stamp duty and penalty, impounding, proof, and relevance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 permits an unregistered document to be received as evidence of a collateral transaction that does not itself require a registered instrument. In a partition suit, collateral use may concern severance of title or the nature of possession, but not division of joint property by metes and bounds. Under Chinnappa Reddy Gari Muthyala Reddy v. Chinnappa Reddy Gari Vankat Reddy, AIR 1969 A.P. 242, an unstamped instrument cannot be admitted even for a collateral purpose until it is impounded; the required stamp duty and penalty must be paid, and proof and relevance remain necessary.

rule.if: partition_suit_evidence_issue and instrument_is_unregistered and instrument_is_unstamped and collateral_use_is_distinct_from_division_by_metes_and_bounds and stamp_duty_and_penalty_paid and instrument_is_impounded

predicates.partition_suit_evidence_issue: The instrument is tendered as evidence in a proceeding seeking partition of property.
predicates.instrument_is_unregistered: The instrument has not been registered.
predicates.instrument_is_unstamped: The instrument has not been duly stamped.
predicates.collateral_use_is_distinct_from_division: The proposed use concerns a matter such as severance of title or the nature of possession, rather than proving division of joint property by metes and bounds.

issues.definition: In a partition proceeding, an unregistered and unstamped instrument can be used for a collateral matter distinct from division by metes and bounds after impounding and payment of stamp duty and penalty, subject to proof and relevance.
